nameStory: The "prickly" part comes from the small spines or ridges that often decorate this little shell's surface, giving it a rougher texture than its smooth cousin, the common jingle shell. The "jingle" name comes from the musical tinkling sound these shells make when washed up in groups on the beach - like nature's own wind chimes!
description: The Prickly Jingle is a small, flattened marine bivalve (clam relative) that lives attached to rocks and other hard surfaces underwater. Unlike typical clams, jingle shells have very thin, translucent shells that feel almost papery when dry. They typically grow to about 1-2 inches across and have an irregular, somewhat circular outline that conforms to whatever surface they're growing on.

idTips.label: Shell texture
idTips.description: Surface feels rough with small ridges, bumps, or spine-like projections - run your finger across it and you'll feel the texture, unlike smooth jingle shells

idTips.label: Attachment hole
idTips.description: Look for a large, round hole in the flatter bottom shell where the animal attached to rocks - it's surprisingly big, often taking up a quarter of the shell

idTips.label: Shell thinness
idTips.description: Incredibly thin and lightweight - you can often see light through the shell, and it may crack easily between your fingers

idTips.label: Color variation
idTips.description: Ranges from golden-yellow to orange, sometimes with darker brown or reddish patches, often with a pearly or iridescent sheen inside

idTips.label: Irregular shape
idTips.description: Shell shape is warped and uneven, molded to fit whatever it was growing on - no two shells look exactly the same

habitat: Found attached to rocks, pilings, and other hard surfaces in shallow coastal waters from the low tide zone down to about 80 feet deep. Most commonly discovered as beach wrack after storms, scattered among seaweed and other shells on sandy or rocky New England beaches.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after spring storms. Living specimens are active underwater as water temperatures begin to warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for beachcombing - shells are commonly found washed up on beaches after summer storms and high tides.
seasonality.fall: Autumn storms bring many shells to shore. This is often the best season for finding well-preserved specimens on the beach.
seasonality.winter: Fewer shells wash ashore, but winter storms can still deposit them. Living animals remain active in deeper, warmer waters.

funFact: Prickly jingles are incredibly strong for such thin shells - they can withstand pounding waves and strong currents by flexing rather than breaking, essentially 'going with the flow' like underwater martial artists!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Common Jingle Shell, but the prickly version has that distinctive rough, ridged texture you can feel with your fingertip. Memory trick: 'Prickly = feels picky' - if it's smooth to touch, it's the common jingle instead.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'shells,' these are often found as single valves rather than pairs since the two halves are very different sizes and the thin top shell breaks away easily from the thicker bottom shell with its attachment hole.
compareHints: As the only Heteranomia species in New England waters, compare it to other jingle shells in the Anomiidae family. The Prickly Jingle is distinguished from Common Jingle Shells by its rougher surface texture and often more irregular, deeply sculpted ridges. It tends to be slightly smaller on average and has more pronounced surface ornamentation than its smooth relatives.
